claim: SARS-CoV-2 is the virus responsible for the COVID-19 pandemic that began in 2019.
source: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is the virus responsible for the COVID-19 pandemic that began in 2019.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge and consensus about the causative agent of COVID-19.

claim: As of early February 2022, COVID-19 has caused 5.7 million deaths worldwide.
source: As of early February 2022, COVID-19 has caused 5.7 million deaths worldwide.
evidence: This is a factual statement about mortality data at a specific time point.

claim: Coronaviruses are enveloped, relatively small (60–140 nm diameter), positive-stranded RNA viruses belonging to the Coronaviridae family.
source: Coronaviruses are enveloped, relatively small (60–140 nm diameter), positive-stranded RNA viruses belonging to the Coronaviridae family.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to V'kovski et al., 2021 and represents established knowledge about coronavirus characteristics.

claim: Coronaviruses derive their name from the crown-like appearance that results from the spike glycoproteins in their envelope.
source: They derive their name from the crown-like appearance (corona means crown in Latin) that results from the spike glycoproteins in their envelope (V'kovski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to V'kovski et al., 2021 and represents established knowledge about coronavirus nomenclature.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 RNA genome is 30 kb long.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 RNA genome is 30 kb long and has 14 open reading frames (ORFs) that encode 29 proteins (16 non-structural proteins, 4 structural proteins, and 9 accessory factors, Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2020 and represents established knowledge about the SARS-CoV-2 genome.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 genome has 14 open reading frames (ORFs) that encode 29 proteins.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 RNA genome is 30 kb long and has 14 open reading frames (ORFs) that encode 29 proteins (16 non-structural proteins, 4 structural proteins, and 9 accessory factors, Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2020 and represents established knowledge about the SARS-CoV-2 genome.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 encodes 16 non-structural proteins, 4 structural proteins, and 9 accessory factors.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 RNA genome is 30 kb long and has 14 open reading frames (ORFs) that encode 29 proteins (16 non-structural proteins, 4 structural proteins, and 9 accessory factors, Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2020 and represents established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 proteins.

claim: The spike glycoprotein on the viral envelope mediates attachment and fusion with the cellular membrane during the first step of viral infection.
source: During the first step of the viral infection, the spike glycoprotein on the viral envelope mediates attachment and fusion with the cellular membrane.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about coronavirus infection mechanisms.

claim: Once the virus is in the cytoplasm of the host cells, the host ribosome machinery is recruited for the synthesis of viral proteins.
source: Once the virus is in the cytoplasm of the host cells, the host ribosome machinery is recruited for the synthesis of viral proteins.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about viral protein synthesis.

claim: Non-structural proteins are required for viral genome replication and are generated by proteolytic cleavage of the polyprotein encoded by ORF1a and ORF1ab.
source: Non-structural proteins are required for viral genome replication and are generated by proteolytic cleavage of the polyprotein encoded by ORF1a and ORF1ab.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about coronavirus non-structural protein generation.

claim: Once the viral genome is replicated, virions are assembled in the host endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi intermediate complex.
source: Once the viral genome is replicated, virions are assembled in the host endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi intermediate complex.
evidence: This is supported by citation to V'kovski et al., 2021 and represents established knowledge about coronavirus assembly.

claim: New viral particles are incorporated into vesicles and secreted by the host cells.
source: Finally, new viral particles are incorporated into vesicles and secreted by the host cells (V'kovski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to V'kovski et al., 2021 and represents established knowledge about coronavirus release.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection elicits a gene expression response that first involves activation of interferon pathway.
source: SARS-CoV-2 infection elicits a peculiar gene expression response that first involves activation of interferon pathway (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Vanderheiden et al., 2020; Wyler et al., 2021), and then the NFkB pathway (Kircheis et al., 2020; Hariharan et al., 2021; Wyler et al., 2021), as well as expression of specific cytokines such as IL6 and IL8 (Wang et al., 2007; Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Coperchini et al., 2020; Park and Lee, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Vanderheiden et al., 2020; Wyler et al., 2021).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection activates the NFkB pathway.
source: SARS-CoV-2 infection elicits a peculiar gene expression response that first involves activation of interferon pathway (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Vanderheiden et al., 2020; Wyler et al., 2021), and then the NFkB pathway (Kircheis et al., 2020; Hariharan et al., 2021; Wyler et al., 2021), as well as expression of specific cytokines such as IL6 and IL8 (Wang et al., 2007; Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Coperchini et al., 2020; Park and Lee, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Kircheis et al., 2020; Hariharan et al., 2021; Wyler et al., 2021).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection induces expression of specific cytokines such as IL6 and IL8.
source: SARS-CoV-2 infection elicits a peculiar gene expression response that first involves activation of interferon pathway (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Vanderheiden et al., 2020; Wyler et al., 2021), and then the NFkB pathway (Kircheis et al., 2020; Hariharan et al., 2021; Wyler et al., 2021), as well as expression of specific cytokines such as IL6 and IL8 (Wang et al., 2007; Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Coperchini et al., 2020; Park and Lee, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Wang et al., 2007; Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Coperchini et al., 2020; Park and Lee, 2020).

claim: The functions of SARS-CoV-2 viral proteins during viral replication are often conserved across coronaviruses.
source: Recent and intense research on SARS-CoV-2 characterized the role of viral proteins during viral replication and showed that these functions are often conserved across coronaviruses (V'kovski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to V'kovski et al., 2021.

claim: Less is known about the roles of the individual SARS-CoV-2 proteins in modulating host cell pathways.
source: Less is known about the roles of the individual proteins in modulating host cell pathways (Gordon et al., 2020a; Gordon et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gordon et al., 2020a and 2020b.

claim: Nsp16 is a splicing modulator.
source: For instance, recent studies have proposed that Nsp16 is a splicing modulator (Banerjee et al., 2020) and that Nsp1 and Nsp14 are translational repressors (Schubert et al., 2020; Hsu, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Banerjee et al., 2020.

claim: Nsp1 and Nsp14 are translational repressors.
source: For instance, recent studies have proposed that Nsp16 is a splicing modulator (Banerjee et al., 2020) and that Nsp1 and Nsp14 are translational repressors (Schubert et al., 2020; Hsu, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schubert et al., 2020 and Hsu, 2021.

claim: Nsp14 is a 60 kDa protein conserved among coronaviruses.
source: Nsp14 is a 60 kDa protein conserved among coronaviruses that is involved both in viral replication and in immune surveillance escape (Ogando et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ogando et al., 2020 and represents established knowledge about Nsp14.

claim: Nsp14 is involved both in viral replication and in immune surveillance escape.
source: Nsp14 is a 60 kDa protein conserved among coronaviruses that is involved both in viral replication and in immune surveillance escape (Ogando et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ogando et al., 2020.

claim: The N-terminal region of Nsp14 contains an exonuclease (ExoN) domain that excises mismatched nucleotides to ensure accurate replication of the viral genome.
source: The N-terminal region of Nsp14 contains an exonuclease (ExoN) domain that excises mismatched nucleotides to ensure accurate replication of the viral genome (Ogando et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ogando et al., 2020.

claim: Coronaviruses have a lower mutation rate than other RNA viruses (error rate of 10^-6 to 10^-7 vs. 10^-3 to 10^-5).
source: As a result of this proofreading mechanism, coronaviruses have a lower mutation rate than other RNA viruses (error rate of 106–107 vs. 103–105) (Sanjuán et al., 2010; Robson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sanjuán et al., 2010 and Robson et al., 2020.

claim: Loss of function of the ExoN domain results in increased sensitivity to the RNA mutagen 5-fluorouracil.
source: Loss of function of the ExoN domain results in increased sensitivity to the RNA mutagen 5-fluorouracil (Eckerle et al., 2010) and attenuated virulence (Graham et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eckerle et al., 2010.

claim: Loss of function of the ExoN domain results in attenuated virulence.
source: Loss of function of the ExoN domain results in increased sensitivity to the RNA mutagen 5-fluorouracil (Eckerle et al., 2010) and attenuated virulence (Graham et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Graham et al., 2012.

claim: The interaction with Nsp10 augments Nsp14 ExoN activity up to 35-fold.
source: Furthermore, the interaction with Nsp10 augments Nsp14 ExoN activity up to 35-fold, and inhibition of the interaction between Nsp10 and Nsp14 leads to reduced replication fidelity (Ma et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ma et al., 2015 and Smith et al., 2015.

claim: Inhibition of the interaction between Nsp10 and Nsp14 leads to reduced replication fidelity.
source: Furthermore, the interaction with Nsp10 augments Nsp14 ExoN activity up to 35-fold, and inhibition of the interaction between Nsp10 and Nsp14 leads to reduced replication fidelity (Ma et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ma et al., 2015 and Smith et al., 2015.

claim: The C-terminal region of Nsp14 functions as an S-adenosyl methionine-dependent guanine-N7 methyl transferase that is independent of the ExoN activity.
source: The C-terminal region of Nsp14 functions as an S-adenosyl methionine-dependent guanine-N7 methyl transferase that is independent of the ExoN activity (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2009.

claim: Both enzymatic domains of Nsp14 are essential for successful viral replication.
source: Both enzymatic domains are essential for successful viral replication, making Nsp14 an appealing drug target (Otava et al., 2021; Saramago et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Otava et al., 2021 and Saramago et al., 2021.

claim: Nsp14 is an appealing drug target.
source: Both enzymatic domains are essential for successful viral replication, making Nsp14 an appealing drug target (Otava et al., 2021; Saramago et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the essential nature of Nsp14 for viral replication, supported by citations.

claim: Replication of SARS-CoV-2 genome takes place in replication organelles that provide a protective environment for the newly synthesized viral genome.
source: As for other coronaviruses, replication of SARS-CoV-2 genome takes place in replication organelles that provide a protective environment for the newly synthesized viral genome (V'kovski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to V'kovski et al., 2021.

claim: Replication organelles are formed in the cytoplasm and present convoluted double layered membranes that likely exchange material with the cytoplasm through pores.
source: Notably, these organelles are formed in the cytoplasm and present convoluted double layered membranes that likely exchange material with the cytoplasm through pores (Wolff et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wolff et al., 2020.

claim: Nsp14 might mediate immune surveillance escape by activating the interferon pathway and activating the pro-inflammatory response through NFkB transcriptional activity and CXCL8 expression.
source: Furthermore, Nsp14 might mediate immune surveillance escape by activating the interferon pathway and activating the pro-inflammatory response through NFkB transcriptional activity and CXCL8 expression (Yuen et al., 2020; Hsu, 2021; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yuen et al., 2020; Hsu, 2021; Li et al., 2021.

claim: The biological mechanism behind Nsp14-mediated immune surveillance escape has not been fully characterized.
source: However, the biological mechanism behind these events has not fully characterized.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Nsp14 interacts with the cellular enzyme inosine-monophosphate dehydrogenase 2 (IMPDH2).
source: Furthermore, a global interactome study showed that Nsp14 interacts with the cellular enzyme inosine-monophosphate dehydrogenase 2 (IMPDH2) and that this interaction is conserved also in SARS-CoV-1 and MERS-CoV viruses (Gordon et al., 2020a; Gordon et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gordon et al., 2020a and 2020b.

claim: The interaction between Nsp14 and IMPDH2 is conserved in SARS-CoV-1 and MERS-CoV viruses.
source: Furthermore, a global interactome study showed that Nsp14 interacts with the cellular enzyme inosine-monophosphate dehydrogenase 2 (IMPDH2) and that this interaction is conserved also in SARS-CoV-1 and MERS-CoV viruses (Gordon et al., 2020a; Gordon et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gordon et al., 2020a and 2020b.

claim: IMPDH2 catalyzes the conversion of inosine-5'-monophosphate (IMP) to xanthine-5'-monophosphate (XMP).
source: IMPDH2 catalyzes the conversion of inosine-5'-monophosphate (IMP) to xanthine-5'-monophosphate (XMP) (Hedstrom, 2009), which is the rate-limiting step of de novo guanine nucleotides biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hedstrom, 2009 and represents established knowledge about IMPDH2 function.

claim: The conversion of IMP to XMP by IMPDH2 is the rate-limiting step of de novo guanine nucleotides biosynthesis.
source: IMPDH2 catalyzes the conversion of inosine-5'-monophosphate (IMP) to xanthine-5'-monophosphate (XMP) (Hedstrom, 2009), which is the rate-limiting step of de novo guanine nucleotides biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hedstrom, 2009 and represents established knowledge about nucleotide biosynthesis.

claim: GTP is necessary for DNA replication and transcription and is used as energy source for translation and as mediator of signal transduction.
source: Guanosine-5'-triphosphate (GTP) is necessary for DNA replication and transcription and is used as energy source for translation and as mediator of signal transduction (Hesketh and Oliver, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hesketh and Oliver, 2019 and represents established knowledge about GTP function.

claim: How the physical interaction between Nsp14 and IMPDH2 impacts the host pathways is not completely understood.
source: How the physical interaction between Nsp14 and IMPDH2 impacts the host pathways is not completely understood (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citation to Li et al., 2021.

claim: Expression of Nsp14 results in global translation inhibition.
source: Interestingly, a recent study has shown that expression of Nsp14 results in global translation inhibition, but it is not clear if this is a direct effect or a downstream consequence of the changes that the expression of this protein provokes to the cellular environment (Hsu, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hsu, 2021.

claim: It is not clear if Nsp14-mediated translation inhibition is a direct effect or a downstream consequence of cellular changes.
source: Interestingly, a recent study has shown that expression of Nsp14 results in global translation inhibition, but it is not clear if this is a direct effect or a downstream consequence of the changes that the expression of this protein provokes to the cellular environment (Hsu, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about uncertainty in the field, supported by citation to Hsu, 2021.

claim: No direct interaction between Nsp14 and ribosomes or a known translational modulator has been reported.
source: Indeed, no direct interaction between Nsp14 and ribosomes or a known translational modulator has been reported, suggesting that the potential translational inhibition might be a downstream effect.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of reported evidence, which is an inference about the state of knowledge.

claim: Expression of Nsp14 altered the expression of about 4000 genes.
source: Expression of Nsp14 altered the expression of about 4000 genes, mostly involved in splicing, RNA metabolism, and cell-cycle control.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Genes altered by Nsp14 expression are mostly involved in splicing, RNA metabolism, and cell-cycle control.
source: Expression of Nsp14 altered the expression of about 4000 genes, mostly involved in splicing, RNA metabolism, and cell-cycle control.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and GO analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The effect of Nsp14 on cellular gene expression resembled the transcriptional changes that occur upon SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Importantly, the effect of Nsp14 on cellular gene expression resembled the transcriptional changes that occur upon SARS-CoV-2 infection and included the activation of the NFkB pathway and the expression of CXCL8 (encoding IL8), a marker of acute severe respiratory distress syndrome in COVID-19 patients (Adcock et al., 2015; Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Kircheis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (GSEA analysis) and citations.

claim: Nsp14 expression activates the NFkB pathway.
source: Importantly, the effect of Nsp14 on cellular gene expression resembled the transcriptional changes that occur upon SARS-CoV-2 infection and included the activation of the NFkB pathway and the expression of CXCL8 (encoding IL8), a marker of acute severe respiratory distress syndrome in COVID-19 patients (Adcock et al., 2015; Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Kircheis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nsp14 expression induces expression of CXCL8 (encoding IL8).
source: Importantly, the effect of Nsp14 on cellular gene expression resembled the transcriptional changes that occur upon SARS-CoV-2 infection and included the activation of the NFkB pathway and the expression of CXCL8 (encoding IL8), a marker of acute severe respiratory distress syndrome in COVID-19 patients (Adcock et al., 2015; Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Kircheis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CXCL8 (IL8) is a marker of acute severe respiratory distress syndrome in COVID-19 patients.
source: Importantly, the effect of Nsp14 on cellular gene expression resembled the transcriptional changes that occur upon SARS-CoV-2 infection and included the activation of the NFkB pathway and the expression of CXCL8 (encoding IL8), a marker of acute severe respiratory distress syndrome in COVID-19 patients (Adcock et al., 2015; Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Kircheis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Adcock et al., 2015; Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Kircheis et al., 2020.

claim: Nsp14 expression increases circRNAs expression.
source: Intriguingly, we also detected an increase in circRNAs expression upon Nsp14 expression; recent studies indicate that circRNAs can act as modulators of the innate immune response during viral infections (Li, 2017; Liu, 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Yan and Chen, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: circRNAs can act as modulators of the innate immune response during viral infections.
source: Intriguingly, we also detected an increase in circRNAs expression upon Nsp14 expression; recent studies indicate that circRNAs can act as modulators of the innate immune response during viral infections (Li, 2017; Liu, 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Yan and Chen, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li, 2017; Liu, 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Yan and Chen, 2020.

claim: IMPDH2 mRNA is downregulated upon Nsp14 expression.
source: Moreover, we showed that the cellular enzyme IMPDH2 mediates the gene expression response induced by Nsp14. We found that IMPDH2 mRNA is downregulated upon Nsp14 expression and that the cellular GTP concentration strongly increases, indicating that Nsp14 might activate IMPDH2 enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cellular GTP concentration strongly increases upon Nsp14 expression.
source: Moreover, we showed that the cellular enzyme IMPDH2 mediates the gene expression response induced by Nsp14. We found that IMPDH2 mRNA is downregulated upon Nsp14 expression and that the cellular GTP concentration strongly increases, indicating that Nsp14 might activate IMPDH2 enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (metabolomic analysis) presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nsp14 might activate IMPDH2 enzymatic activity.
source: Moreover, we showed that the cellular enzyme IMPDH2 mediates the gene expression response induced by Nsp14. We found that IMPDH2 mRNA is downregulated upon Nsp14 expression and that the cellular GTP concentration strongly increases, indicating that Nsp14 might activate IMPDH2 enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed downregulation of IMPDH2 mRNA and increased GTP levels.

claim: Treatment with IMPDH2 inhibitors (mycophenolic acid and mizoribine) partially rescued the changes in gene expression induced by Nsp14.
source: In accordance with our hypothesis, we showed that treatment with IMPDH2 inhibitors (mycophenolic acid [MPA] and mizoribine [MZR], Lee et al., 2020a), partially rescued the changes in gene expression induced by Nsp14.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Expression of most SARS-CoV-2 proteins resulted in modest or no changes in the transcriptome of HEK293T cells.
source: Interestingly, expression of most proteins resulted in modest or no changes in the transcriptome of the HEK293T cells. Indeed, we detected less than 300 DEGs upon expression of 17 of the 25 tested proteins (Supplementary file 1a and Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Less than 300 DEGs were detected upon expression of 17 of the 25 tested SARS-CoV-2 proteins.
source: Interestingly, expression of most proteins resulted in modest or no changes in the transcriptome of the HEK293T cells. Indeed, we detected less than 300 DEGs upon expression of 17 of the 25 tested proteins (Supplementary file 1a and Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of seven viral proteins (M, Nsp9, E, ORF9b, ORF3a, Nsp13, and Nsp1) modestly altered the transcriptome (between 300 and 700 DEGs).
source: Expression of seven viral proteins, M, Nsp9, E, ORF9b, ORF3a, Nsp13, and Nsp1, modestly altered the transcriptome (between 300 and 700 DEGs).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: DEGs upon expression of M, Nsp9, E, ORF9b, ORF3a, Nsp13, and Nsp1 tended to be upregulated rather than downregulated.
source: Interestingly, these DEGs tended to be upregulated rather than downregulated (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Nsp14 altered the expression of more than 4000 RNAs (1862 upregulated and 2161 downregulated).
source: Striking, Nsp14 altered the expression of more than 4000 RNAs (1862 upregulated and 2161 downregulated; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The profound impact of Nsp14 expression on the transcriptome suggests that this protein has roles beyond its known functions in viral genome proofreading and immune system escape.
source: The profound impact of Nsp14 expression on the transcriptome of HEK293T cells suggests that this protein has roles beyond its known functions in viral genome proofreading and immune system escape.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing extensive transcriptome changes.

claim: Expression of Nsp7 deregulated expression of genes encoding proteins involved in DNA and RNA metabolism.
source: For example, expression of Nsp7, an accessory protein of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (Kirchdoerfer and Ward, 2019; Hillen, 2020), deregulated expression of genes encoding proteins involved in DNA and RNA metabolism (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (GO analysis) presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Nsp7 is an accessory protein of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
source: For example, expression of Nsp7, an accessory protein of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (Kirchdoerfer and Ward, 2019; Hillen, 2020), deregulated expression of genes encoding proteins involved in DNA and RNA metabolism (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kirchdoerfer and Ward, 2019; Hillen, 2020.

claim: Expression of Nsp9 and Nsp13 resulted in the mis-regulation of mRNAs encoding proteins involved in RNA metabolism and translation.
source: Expression of Nsp9 and Nsp13, known to bind RNA and to regulate RNA metabolism, respectively (Egloff et al., 2004; Shu et al., 2020), resulted in the mis-regulation of mRNAs encoding proteins involved in RNA metabolism and translation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (GO analysis) presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Nsp9 is known to bind RNA.
source: Expression of Nsp9 and Nsp13, known to bind RNA and to regulate RNA metabolism, respectively (Egloff et al., 2004; Shu et al., 2020), resulted in the mis-regulation of mRNAs encoding proteins involved in RNA metabolism and translation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Egloff et al., 2004; Shu et al., 2020.

claim: Nsp13 is known to regulate RNA metabolism.
source: Expression of Nsp9 and Nsp13, known to bind RNA and to regulate RNA metabolism, respectively (Egloff et al., 2004; Shu et al., 2020), resulted in the mis-regulation of mRNAs encoding proteins involved in RNA metabolism and translation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Egloff et al., 2004; Shu et al., 2020.

claim: Expression of ORF3d resulted in alteration of genes involved in cell metabolism and immunity.
source: Furthermore, expression of the protein ORF3d, known to bind STOML2 mitochondrial protein, may be a unique antigenic target upon SARS-CoV-2 infection (Gordon et al., 2020b; Hachim et al., 2020; Nelson et al., 2020; Jungreis et al., 2021), resulted in alteration of genes involved in cell metabolism and immunity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (GO analysis) presented in Figure 1C.

claim: ORF3d is known to bind STOML2 mitochondrial protein.
source: Furthermore, expression of the protein ORF3d, known to bind STOML2 mitochondrial protein, may be a unique antigenic target upon SARS-CoV-2 infection (Gordon et al., 2020b; Hachim et al., 2020; Nelson et al., 2020; Jungreis et al., 2021), resulted in alteration of genes involved in cell metabolism and immunity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gordon et al., 2020b; Hachim et al., 2020; Nelson et al., 2020; Jungreis et al., 2021.

claim: ORF3d may be a unique antigenic target upon SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Furthermore, expression of the protein ORF3d, known to bind STOML2 mitochondrial protein, may be a unique antigenic target upon SARS-CoV-2 infection (Gordon et al., 2020b; Hachim et al., 2020; Nelson et al., 2020; Jungreis et al., 2021), resulted in alteration of genes involved in cell metabolism and immunity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gordon et al., 2020b; Hachim et al., 2020; Nelson et al., 2020; Jungreis et al., 2021.

claim: Expression of viral proteins mainly impacted pathways related to RNA metabolism, translation, and cell metabolism.
source: In general, expression of the viral proteins mainly impacted pathways related to RNA metabolism, translation, and cell metabolism that were previously reported to be affected upon viral infection (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Gardinassi et al., 2020; Wyler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (GO analysis) and citations.

claim: Expression of Nsp14 affected the expression of genes involved in RNA splicing, metabolism, and processing, translation, cell-cycle control, and the cytoskeleton.
source: Expression of Nsp14 affected the expression of genes involved in RNA splicing, metabolism, and processing, translation, cell-cycle control, and the cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (GO analysis) presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Nsp14 impacted the expression of genes involved in general metabolism, especially genes implicated in nucleotide metabolism.
source: Nsp14 also impacted the expression of genes involved in general metabolism, especially on genes implicated in nucleotide metabolism (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (GO analysis) presented in Figure 1C.

claim: The total RNA-seq dataset strongly resembled the 3' RNA-seq dataset for Nsp14 expression.
source: The new dataset strongly resembled the one obtained by 3' RNA-seq (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1c, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) but also contained information about the full-length RNAs, non-poly-adenylated RNAs, and pre-mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: For genes upregulated upon expression of Nsp14, three of the four most highly enriched GSEA datasets were those of cells infected with SARS-CoV-2.
source: Strikingly, we found that for genes upregulated upon expression of Nsp14, three of the four most highly enriched GSEA datasets were those of cells infected with SARS-CoV-2 (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Figure 2B and C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (GSEA analysis) presented in Figure 2B and C.

claim: There is a smaller but significant enrichment of genes upregulated upon infection with MERS in the Nsp14 expression dataset.
source: Moreover, we observed a smaller but significant enrichment of genes upregulated upon infection with MERS, a related virus (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (GSEA analysis) and citation to Blanco-Melo et al., 2020.

claim: The mRNAs downregulated upon expression of Nsp14 tended to be strongly enriched for those downregulated following SARS-CoV-2 viral infection.
source: Further, the mRNAs downregulated upon expression of Nsp14 tended to be strongly enriched for those downregulated following SARS-CoV-2 viral infection (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (GSEA analysis) presented in Figure 2B.

claim: No enrichment was detected when the Nsp14 dataset was compared to data from cells infected with influenza A virus.
source: We did not detect enrichment when our dataset were compared to data from cells infected with influenza A virus (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (GSEA analysis) presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Expression of a single viral protein (Nsp14) can recapitulate a considerable portion of response of a host cell to SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: These results demonstrate that expression of a single viral protein can recapitulate a considerable portion of response of a host cell to SARS-CoV-2 infection and highlights the potential importance of Nsp14 in hijacking host gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GSEA analysis showing overlap with SARS-CoV-2 infection datasets.

claim: Nsp14 is potentially important in hijacking host gene expression during SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: These results demonstrate that expression of a single viral protein can recapitulate a considerable portion of response of a host cell to SARS-CoV-2 infection and highlights the potential importance of Nsp14 in hijacking host gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing extensive transcriptome changes that resemble infection.

claim: A large part of the transcriptome response to Nsp14 is transcriptional.
source: We observed a strong correlation (R = 0.73 and p-value = 2.2e−16) between these two measures (Figure 2D), indicating that a large part of the response is transcriptional.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (intronic signal analysis) presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Of the 1862 genes upregulated upon Nsp14 expression, 1006 also had higher intronic signal.
source: For example, of the 1862 genes that were upregulated upon Nsp14 expression, 1006 also had higher intronic signal (at least 20% signal increase), whereas only 57 of the showed decreased intronic signal.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Of the 2161 genes downregulated upon Nsp14 expression, 1242 displayed lower intronic signal.
source: Similarly, of the 2161 genes downregulated upon Nsp14 expression, 1242 displayed lower intronic signal (at least 20% signal decrease), whereas only 109 showed higher intronic signal (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Supplementary file 1d.

claim: More than 50% of the changes in the transcriptome upon Nsp14 expression are transcriptional.
source: In sum, we observed that more than 50% of the changes in the transcriptome upon Nsp14 expression are transcriptional.
evidence: This is an inference based on the intronic signal analysis data.

claim: Genes upregulated upon Nsp14 expression (FGF-18 and CXCL8) were also upregulated in the chromatin-bound fraction.
source: Genes upregulated upon Nsp14 expression (FGF-18 and CXCL8) were also upregulated in the chromatin-bound fraction, while the downregulated ones (SH2D2A and COL13A) were downregulated indicating that at least those mRNAs are regulated at the transcriptional level by Nsp14.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (RT-qPCR on chromatin-bound RNA) presented in Figure 2F.

claim: Genes downregulated upon Nsp14 expression (SH2D2A and COL13A) were downregulated in the chromatin-bound fraction.
source: Genes upregulated upon Nsp14 expression (FGF-18 and CXCL8) were also upregulated in the chromatin-bound fraction, while the downregulated ones (SH2D2A and COL13A) were downregulated indicating that at least those mRNAs are regulated at the transcriptional level by Nsp14.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (RT-qPCR on chromatin-bound RNA) presented in Figure 2F.

claim: The gene expression changes observed upon Nsp14 expression are mainly transcriptional.
source: These results verify the genomic observations and strongly suggest that the gene expression changes observed upon Nsp14 are mainly transcriptional (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (intronic signal analysis and chromatin-bound RNA analysis).

claim: More than 1000 genes display higher intronic signals with no changes in gene expression upon Nsp14 expression.
source: Interestingly, we also observed that there are more than 1000 genes that display higher intronic signals with no changes in gene expression, indicating that, in addition to the transcriptional effects, Nsp14 might also affect splicing (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Supplementary file 1e.

claim: Nsp14 might affect splicing in addition to transcriptional effects.
source: Interestingly, we also observed that there are more than 1000 genes that display higher intronic signals with no changes in gene expression, indicating that, in addition to the transcriptional effects, Nsp14 might also affect splicing (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased intronic signal without changes in mRNA levels.

claim: Expression of Nsp14 strongly altered the inclusion patterns of almost 2300 exons.
source: Indeed, we found that expression of Nsp14 strongly altered the inclusion patterns of almost 2300 exons, with more than 2000 exons displaying lower inclusion in the mature mRNA and 238 showing higher levels of inclusion when we expressed Nsp14 (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1e, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (alternative splicing analysis) presented in Figure 3A.

claim: More than 2000 exons displayed lower inclusion in the mature mRNA upon Nsp14 expression.
source: Indeed, we found that expression of Nsp14 strongly altered the inclusion patterns of almost 2300 exons, with more than 2000 exons displaying lower inclusion in the mature mRNA and 238 showing higher levels of inclusion when we expressed Nsp14 (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1e, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: 238 exons showed higher levels of inclusion upon Nsp14 expression.
source: Indeed, we found that expression of Nsp14 strongly altered the inclusion patterns of almost 2300 exons, with more than 2000 exons displaying lower inclusion in the mature mRNA and 238 showing higher levels of inclusion when we expressed Nsp14 (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1e, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Nsp14 expression results in genes using alternative acceptor or donor splice sites.
source: Furthermore, we also identified genes which used alternative acceptor or donor splice sites upon expression of Nsp14 (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: There is an increase in the retention of more than 2000 introns following Nsp14 expression.
source: Moreover, we observed an increase in the retention of more than 2000 introns following Nsp14 expression (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3A and C.

claim: Most of the introns with increased retention are within genes that were not differentially expressed.
source: However, as most of the introns with increased retention are within genes that were not differentially expressed (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), we reasoned that expression of Nsp14 leads to changes in splicing in this subset of genes as well.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The effect of Nsp14 on alternative splicing appears to be specific to particular introns and exons in each gene.
source: Moreover, the effect of Nsp14 on alternative splicing appears to be specific to particular introns and exons in each gene, as the majority (~62%) of identified genes had a single spicing event altered (Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: The majority (~62%) of genes with altered splicing had a single splicing event altered.
source: Moreover, the effect of Nsp14 on alternative splicing appears to be specific to particular introns and exons in each gene, as the majority (~62%) of identified genes had a single spicing event altered (Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Most genes with altered splicing do not show expression changes upon Nsp14 expression.
source: Notably, most genes with altered splicing do not show expression changes upon Nsp14 expression, further indicating that the detected alternative splicing events are independent to transcriptional changes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The affected introns by Nsp14 tended to be at the 5' end of the transcript.
source: Interestingly, we found that the affected introns tended to be at the 5' end of the transcript and were embedded in genomic regions with higher-than-average GC content (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The affected introns by Nsp14 were embedded in genomic regions with higher-than-average GC content.
source: Interestingly, we found that the affected introns tended to be at the 5' end of the transcript and were embedded in genomic regions with higher-than-average GC content (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Most of the affected exons by Nsp14 are shorter and have higher GC content around their splice sites than a randomized subset of exons not affected by Nsp14.
source: Furthermore, most of the affected exons are shorter and have higher GC content around their splice sites than a randomized subset of exons not affected by Nsp14 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Higher GC content suggests that stable RNA structures form around the splice sites in affected exons, which correlates with alternative splicing propensity.
source: The higher GC content suggests that stable RNA structures form around the splice sites in these exon, which correlates with alternative splicing propensity (Zhang et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed GC content and citations to Zhang et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2016.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection disrupts splicing, mostly by inducing intron retention.
source: Previous research showed that SARS-CoV-2 infection disrupts splicing, mostly by inducing intron retention (Banerjee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Banerjee et al., 2020.

claim: There is a significant overlap between the alternative splicing events during SARS-CoV-2 infection and in the Nsp14 expression model.
source: We found that there is a significant overlap (p-value < 0.01, see Materials and methods) between the alternative splicing events during the infection and in our model.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (re-analysis of published dataset).

claim: 10% of the alternative splicing events changing with SARS-CoV-2 infection also change (and in the same direction) when Nsp14 is expressed.
source: Specifically, 10% of the alternative splicing events changing with SARS-CoV-2 infection (Supplementary file 1g) also change (and in the same direction) when we express Nsp14 (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (re-analysis of published dataset).

claim: Expression of Nsp14 partially recapitulates the gene expression changes and some of the alternative splicing events that occur upon SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: In sum, we showed that expression of Nsp14 partially recapitulates the gene expression changes, as well as some of the alternative splicing events that occur upon SARS-CoV-2 infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GSEA and alternative splicing overlap analyses.

claim: There is a strong increase (more than twofold) in the total number of circRNA reads upon Nsp14 expression.
source: Using the total RNA-seq data, we found that there is a strong increase (more than twofold) in the total number of circRNA reads upon Nsp14 expression (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: Most of the 246 circRNAs that were differentially expressed upon expression of Nsp14 were upregulated.
source: Most of the 246 circRNAs that were differentially expressed upon expression of Nsp14 were upregulated (put the number of upregulated; Figure 3F and Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: The levels of most of the mRNAs that host upregulated circRNAs were unchanged upon Nsp14 expression.
source: Interestingly, the levels of most of the mRNAs that host these circRNAs were unchanged (Figure 3G and Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3G.

claim: Nsp14 did not increase the transcription of loci hosting the upregulated circRNAs.
source: Indeed, Nsp14 did not increase the transcription of loci hosting the upregulated circRNAs (we observed increased levels of intronic sequences in only 20 out of the 190 loci with upregulated circRNAs; Figure 3H and Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3H.

claim: The increased circRNA levels upon Nsp14 expression are caused by increased biosynthesis or stability of the circRNAs.
source: Together, these results strongly suggest that the increased circRNA levels are caused by increased biosynthesis or stability of the circRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that host mRNA levels and transcription are not increased.

claim: Expression of Nsp14 influences alternative splicing and back-splicing on the host cells.
source: In sum, our data shows that expression of Nsp14 influences alternative splicing and back-splicing on the host cells.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data on alternative splicing and circRNA expression.

claim: Co-expression of Nsp14 and Nsp10 did not impact levels of Nsp14 protein.
source: Co-expression of Nsp14 and Nsp10 did not impact levels of Nsp14 protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (Western blot) presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Expression of Nsp10 alone or in combination with Nsp14 did not further alter the levels of mRNAs tested compared to Nsp14 alone.
source: Interestingly, expression of Nsp10 alone or in combination with Nsp14 did not further alter the levels of any of the mRNAs tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (RT-qPCR) presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of only Nsp10 did not considerably alter the gene expression profile (only 88 DEGs).
source: Unlike expression of Nsp14, which provoked a strong remodeling of the mRNA and circRNA populations (Figures 1—3), expression of Nsp10 did not considerably alter the gene expression profile (only 88 DEGs, Figure 4B and C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The gene expression profiles of cells transfected with Nsp14 alone or in combination with Nsp10 are strikingly similar.
source: As also suggested by the RT-qPCR experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), the gene expression profiles of cells transfected with Nsp14 alone or in combination with Nsp10 are strikingly similar.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (RNA-seq and RT-qPCR).

claim: There is an almost complete overlap between the DEGs resulting from Nsp14 expression and from co-expression of Nsp14 and Nsp10.
source: Indeed, we observed an almost complete overlap between the DEGs resulting from Nsp14 expression and from co-expression of Nsp14 and Nsp10, and there was a very strong correlation between the fold change in DEGs upon Nsp14 expression with and without Nsp10 co-expression (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Co-expression of Nsp10 did not result in additional differentially expressed mRNAs compared to expression of Nsp14 alone.
source: Moreover, co-expression of Nsp10 did not result in additional differentially expressed mRNAs (Figure 4B and C) and did not alter of the number of circRNAs reads (Figure 4D) compared to expression of Nsp14 alone.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 4B, C, and D.

claim: Co-expression of Nsp10 did not alter the number of circRNAs reads compared to expression of Nsp14 alone.
source: Moreover, co-expression of Nsp10 did not result in additional differentially expressed mRNAs (Figure 4B and C) and did not alter of the number of circRNAs reads (Figure 4D) compared to expression of Nsp14 alone.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: The Nsp14 ExoN activity is not responsible for the dramatic effects of Nsp14 expression on the transcriptome.
source: These data strongly suggests that the Nsp14 ExoN activity is not responsible for the dramatic effects of Nsp14 expression on the transcriptome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no additional effects with Nsp10 co-expression.

claim: The mutations D90A/G92A and D273A in the ExoN domain completely inhibit the ExoN activity of Nsp14.
source: These mutations have been previously shown to completely inhibit the ExoN activity of Nsp14 (Ma et al., 2015; Ogando et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ma et al., 2015; Ogando et al., 2020.

claim: The mutations in the ExoN domain did not alter the strong effects induced by Nsp14 expression.
source: The mutations in the ExoN domain did not alter the strong effects induced by Nsp14 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C) and the fold changes in mRNA expression induced upon expression of the wild-type or mutated Nsp14 were also strikingly similar (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The fold changes in mRNA expression induced upon expression of the wild-type or ExoN-mutated Nsp14 were strikingly similar.
source: The mutations in the ExoN domain did not alter the strong effects induced by Nsp14 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C) and the fold changes in mRNA expression induced upon expression of the wild-type or mutated Nsp14 were also strikingly similar (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: No significant differences in the expression of three tested circRNAs were detected between samples that expressed the wild-type Nsp14 and the ExoN mutants.
source: Moreover, we did not detect significant differences in the expression of the three tested circRNAs between samples that expressed the wild-type Nsp14 (Nsp14 WT) and the ExoN mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The ExoN activity of Nsp14 is not required for the observed transcriptome effects.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the ExoN activity of Nsp14 is not required for the observed transcriptome effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data with ExoN mutants.

claim: Overexpression of Nsp14 D331A does not alter the expression of tested mRNA and circRNA targets.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of Nsp14 D331A does not alter the expression of the tested targets (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (RT-qPCR) presented in Figure 4G and H.

claim: The lack of effect of Nsp14 D331A is not due to low expression or stability of the mutant protein.
source: The lack of effect is not due to low expression or stability of the Nsp14 D331A mutant, as it was expressed at similar levels than Nsp14 WT as assessed by Western blot (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (Western blot) presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The N7-guanine-methyltransferase domain of Nsp14 is required for driving the gene expression changes.
source: In summary, our results indicate that the N7-guanine-methyltransferase domain of Nsp14 is required for driving the gene expression changes described in this study.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data with the D331A mutant.

claim: Detectable levels of Nsp14 mRNA and protein were observed even early after transfection (6 hours).
source: Importantly, we observed detectable levels of Nsp14 mRNA and protein even early after transfection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The effect of Nsp14 expression dramatically increased over time with a gradual increase in the number of DEGs.
source: The effect of Nsp14 expression dramatically increased over time with a gradual increase in the number of DEGs (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, and Supplementary file 2a), as well as an increase in the number of significantly enriched GO terms (Figure 5C and Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (time course RNA-seq) presented in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Expression of genes related to cell metabolism, RNA metabolism, and cell cycle were altered relative to the control only at 24 and 48 hr post transfection.
source: For example, expression of genes related to cell metabolism, RNA metabolism, and cell cycle were altered relative to the control only at 24 and 48 hr post transfection (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (GO analysis) presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Only 19 DEGs were observed at the 8 hr time point after Nsp14 transfection.
source: We observed only 19 DEGs at the 8 hr time point and 200 DEGs at the 12 hr time point (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: 200 DEGs were observed at the 12 hr time point after Nsp14 transfection.
source: We observed only 19 DEGs at the 8 hr time point and 200 DEGs at the 12 hr time point (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: CXCL8 was the most highly induced mRNA at the 8 hr time point (fold change = 11.5, p-value = 1.2e–5).
source: Interestingly, CXCL8, which encodes IL8, was the most highly induced mRNA at the 8 hr time point (fold change = 11.5, p-value = 1.2e–5, Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Supplementary file 1h.

claim: CXCL8 was induced by more than 12-fold consistently between 8 and 48 hr post transfection.
source: Furthermore, we found that CXCL8 was induced by more than 12-fold consistently between 8 and 48 hr post transfection (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: CXCL8 mRNA is significantly upregulated following infection of cells with SARS-CoV-2.
source: It was previously reported that CXCL8 mRNA is significantly upregulated following infection of cells with SARS-CoV-2 and that the levels of IL8 are increased in COVID-19 patients (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Coperchini et al., 2020; Del Valle et al., 2020; Gardinassi et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Coperchini et al., 2020; Del Valle et al., 2020; Gardinassi et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021.

claim: The levels of IL8 are increased in COVID-19 patients.
source: It was previously reported that CXCL8 mRNA is significantly upregulated following infection of cells with SARS-CoV-2 and that the levels of IL8 are increased in COVID-19 patients (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Coperchini et al., 2020; Del Valle et al., 2020; Gardinassi et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Coperchini et al., 2020; Del Valle et al., 2020; Gardinassi et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021.

claim: Expression of Nsp14 led to an almost fourfold increase in the signal from the CXCL8 promoter luciferase reporter.
source: Expression of Nsp14 led to an almost fourfold increase in the signal from the luciferase reporter (Figure 5E), indicating that Nsp14 expression activates CXCL8 transcription.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (luciferase assay) presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Nsp14 expression activates CXCL8 transcription.
source: Expression of Nsp14 led to an almost fourfold increase in the signal from the luciferase reporter (Figure 5E), indicating that Nsp14 expression activates CXCL8 transcription.
evidence: This is an inference based on the luciferase reporter assay data.

claim: CXCL8 expression is controlled by several transcription factors, including NFkB.
source: CXCL8 expression is controlled by several transcription factors (TFs), including NFkB, a master regulator of inflammation (Kunsch and Rosen, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kunsch and Rosen, 1993 and represents established knowledge.

claim: NFkB is a master regulator of inflammation.
source: CXCL8 expression is controlled by several transcription factors (TFs), including NFkB, a master regulator of inflammation (Kunsch and Rosen, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kunsch and Rosen, 1993 and represents established knowledge.

claim: NFkB is activated during infections with SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2.
source: Recent reports have shown that NFkB is activated during infections with SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2, although the mechanism and the importance of this activation are not well established (Liao, 2005; Kircheis et al., 2020; Park and Lee, 2020; Hariharan et al., 2021; Hsu, 2021; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liao, 2005; Kircheis et al., 2020; Park and Lee, 2020; Hariharan et al., 2021; Hsu, 2021; Li et al., 2021.

claim: The mechanism and the importance of NFkB activation during SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 infections are not well established.
source: Recent reports have shown that NFkB is activated during infections with SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2, although the mechanism and the importance of this activation are not well established (Liao, 2005; Kircheis et al., 2020; Park and Lee, 2020; Hariharan et al., 2021; Hsu, 2021; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Some of the top upregulated RNAs at 8 hr post transfection of Nsp14 were NFKBIA, JUN, and ATF3.
source: Strikingly, some of the top upregulated RNAs at 8 hr post transfection of Nsp14 were NFKBIA, JUN, and ATF3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), which encode proteins involved in the activation and modulation of the NFkB pathway (Stein et al., 1993; Baldwin, 1996; Pahl, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: NFKBIA, JUN, and ATF3 encode proteins involved in the activation and modulation of the NFkB pathway.
source: Strikingly, some of the top upregulated RNAs at 8 hr post transfection of Nsp14 were NFKBIA, JUN, and ATF3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), which encode proteins involved in the activation and modulation of the NFkB pathway (Stein et al., 1993; Baldwin, 1996; Pahl, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stein et al., 1993; Baldwin, 1996; Pahl, 1999.

claim: There is a significant enrichment in promoters of genes upregulated at 8 hr for binding sites recognized by components of the NFkB transcription complex and the NFkB regulatory network.
source: We found a significant enrichment in those promoters for binding sites recognized by components of the NFkB transcription complex and the NFkB regulatory network (Figure 5F, Supplementary file 2c, and d, Stein et al., 1993; Baldwin, 1996; Pahl, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (motif enrichment analysis) presented in Figure 5F.

claim: Expression of Nsp14 led to an approximately 1.6-fold increase in the luciferase signal from an NFkB reporter.
source: Indeed, we observed that expression of Nsp14 lead to an approximately 1.6-fold increase in the luciferase signal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F), demonstrating that this viral protein activates the NFkB pathway.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (luciferase assay) presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Nsp14 activates the NFkB pathway.
source: Indeed, we observed that expression of Nsp14 lead to an approximately 1.6-fold increase in the luciferase signal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F), demonstrating that this viral protein activates the NFkB pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NFkB reporter assay data.

claim: Extended promoter regions of mRNAs strongly upregulated early after Nsp14 transfection were enriched for binding sites for factors involved in the interferon response such as EGR2, STAT2, and SP3.
source: We found that these regions were enriched for binding sites for factors involved in the interferon response such as EGR2, STAT2, and SP3 (Supplementary file 2e).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (motif enrichment analysis) presented in Supplementary file 2e.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection modulates both the interferon and the NFkB pathways.
source: Previous work showed that SARS-CoV-2 infection modulates both the interferon and the NFkB pathways (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Vanderheiden et al., 2020; Wyler et al., 2021) and that Nsp14 affects these pathways (Hsu, 2021; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Vanderheiden et al., 2020; Wyler et al., 2021.

claim: Nsp14 affects the interferon and NFkB pathways.
source: Previous work showed that SARS-CoV-2 infection modulates both the interferon and the NFkB pathways (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Vanderheiden et al., 2020; Wyler et al., 2021) and that Nsp14 affects these pathways (Hsu, 2021; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hsu, 2021; Li et al., 2021.

claim: The initial response to Nsp14 expression involves modulation of both the NFkB and the interferon pathways.
source: Our data indicates that the initial response to Nsp14 expression involves modulation of both the NFkB and the interferon pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the motif enrichment analysis and luciferase assay data.

claim: Nsp14 localizes in the cytoplasm when expressed in HEK293T cells.
source: However, previous research showed that Nsp14 localizes in the cytoplasm when expressed in HEK293T cells (Gordon et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gordon et al., 2020a.

claim: Nsp14 localizes in the cytoplasm and does not associate with chromatin.
source: We then performed subcellular fractionation and chromatin purification, followed by Western blot at different time points after transfection, and we showed that Nsp14 localizes in the cytoplasm, and it does not associate with chromatin demonstrating that the transcriptional effect is indirect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (subcellular fractionation and Western blot) presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The transcriptional effect of Nsp14 is indirect.
source: We then performed subcellular fractionation and chromatin purification, followed by Western blot at different time points after transfection, and we showed that Nsp14 localizes in the cytoplasm, and it does not associate with chromatin demonstrating that the transcriptional effect is indirect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Nsp14 does not associate with chromatin.

claim: Expression of Nsp14 changed the levels of genes involved in purine metabolism.
source: One possibility is that Nsp14 activates IMPDH2 which then modulates gene expression directly or indirectly. In support of this possibility, expression of Nsp14 changed the levels of genes involved in purine metabolism (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (GO analysis) presented in Figure 1C.

claim: IMPDH2 mRNA expression is significantly downregulated upon Nsp14 expression.
source: Furthermore, we found IMPDH2 mRNA expression significantly downregulated upon Nsp14 expression (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: GTP levels inversely regulate IMPDH2 expression.
source: As GTP levels inversely regulate IMPDH2 expression (Glesne et al., 1991), we hypothesized that Nsp14 promotes the activation of IMPDH2, leading to higher GTP levels that, in the end, negatively regulate IMPDH2 mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Glesne et al., 1991.

claim: An approximately threefold increase in the levels of xanthine diphosphate and GTP was detected upon Nsp14 expression.
source: Consistent with modulation of IMPDH2 activity by Nsp14, we detected an approximately threefold increase in the levels of xanthine diphosphate and GTP (Figure 6B and Supplementary file 3a), the downstream products of XMP.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (metabolomic analysis) presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Increased concentrations of other nucleotides that directly or indirectly derive from IMP were observed upon Nsp14 expression.
source: Furthermore, we observed increased concentrations of other nucleotides that directly or indirectly derive from IMP (Figure 6B and Supplementary file 3a), probably due to activated compensatory pathways.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (metabolomic analysis) presented in Figure 6B.

claim: MPA treatment diminishes the effects induced by expression of Nsp14.
source: Interestingly, we observed that MPA treatment diminishes the effects induced by expression of Nsp14 (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data (RNA-seq with MPA treatment) presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Only 115 DEGs were detected in cells treated with MPA compared to control cells.
source: We detected only 115 DEGs in cells treated with MPA compared to control cells.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In cells expressing Nsp14, 3761 DEGs were detected.
source: In cells expressing Nsp14, we detected 3761 DEGs.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There were only 1245 DEGs in cells expressing Nsp14 that were treated with MPA compared to control cells.
source: By contrast, there were only 1245 DEGs in cells expressing Nsp14 that we treated with MPA compared to control cells, demonstrating that about 73% of the changes depends on the activity of IMPDH2 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: About 73% of the gene expression changes induced by Nsp14 depend on the activity of IMPDH2.
source: By contrast, there were only 1245 DEGs in cells expressing Nsp14 that we treated with MPA compared to control cells, demonstrating that about 73% of the changes depends on the activity of IMPDH2 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of DEG numbers with and without MPA treatment.

claim: Approximately 1000 genes were deregulated in cells expressing Nsp14 with or without MPA.
source: Approximately 1000 genes were deregulated in cells expressing Nsp14 with or without MPA (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: MPA treatment mitigates the effects of Nsp14 even in mRNAs that are still differentially expressed in the presence of the drug.
source: In addition, the effect of those genes still differentially expressed was smaller in the presence of MPA. This can be seen by comparing the distribution of fold changes of the DEGs (Figure 6F). When we treated cells expressing Nsp14 with MPA, the distribution of fold change narrowed, indicating that MPA treatment mitigates the effects of Nsp14 even in those mRNAs that are still differentially expressed in the presence of the drug.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 6F.

claim: A similar, milder, effect of Nsp14 expression was observed when assaying the levels of a subset of circRNAs in the presence of MPA.
source: Moreover, we observed a similar, milder, effect of Nsp14 expression when assaying the levels of a subset of circRNAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: MZR treatment partially rescued the expression of tested mRNAs and circRNAs deregulated by Nsp14 overexpression.
